name: Adenosine kinase deficiency
aliases: hypermethioninaemia due to adenosine kinase deficiency

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of adenosine kinase, which phosphorylates adenosine to AMP and is closely coupled to the transmethylation cycle
Removing adenosine normally pulls S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolysis forward, so enzyme deficiency disturbs methionine metabolism and produces hypermethioninaemia
Presents with a distinctive combination of encephalopathy, global developmental delay and hypotonia
Characteristic additional features include dysmorphic facies, hepatic dysfunction and hypoglycaemia, sometimes with hyperinsulinism
Cardiac and, less often, other organ involvement can accompany the neurological and hepatic picture
Biochemically there is raised methionine with elevated S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine and often increased adenosine
It belongs to the group of methylation-cycle defects that must be separated from the benign hypermethioninaemias
Management is generic and largely supportive, with a methionine-restricted diet used to lower the toxic accumulation
reference.pathophysiology: Adenosine kinase salvages adenosine by phosphorylating it to AMP. This reaction is important not only for purine handling but also for transmethylation, because clearance of adenosine helps drive the hydrolysis of S-adenosylhomocysteine to homocysteine and adenosine. When adenosine kinase is deficient, adenosine accumulates and the transmethylation cycle is impeded, so S-adenosylhomocysteine, S-adenosylmethionine and methionine all rise and cellular methylation is impaired. The resulting disturbance of methylation-dependent processes, together with effects on hepatic and pancreatic function, is thought to underlie the encephalopathy, liver dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and dysmorphism.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital disorders of glycosylation presenting with dysmorphism and hepatopathy
Neonatal liver disease with secondary hypermethioninaemia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing raised methionine
Liver function tests and coagulation studies
Blood glucose and insulin during hypoglycaemia
Brain MRI to characterise the encephalopathy
redFlags: Recurrent or persistent hypoglycaemia, particularly with hyperinsulinism
reference.prognosis: The disorder is typically serious, with substantial neurodevelopmental impairment in many patients; treatment is largely supportive, and outcome depends on the severity of encephalopathy, liver disease and metabolic instability.
pitfalls: Overlooking it among the hypermethioninaemias because the biochemical overlap with AHCY deficiency is close
Attributing the hypoglycaemia solely to hyperinsulinism without recognising the underlying metabolic disorder
Ascribing the dysmorphism and hepatopathy to an unrelated syndrome
Failing to measure the methylation-cycle metabolites needed to place the diagnosis
references: Bjursell MK et al. Adenosine kinase deficiency disrupts the methionine cycle
Mudd SH. Hypermethioninemias of genetic and non-genetic origin
management: Provide supportive multidisciplinary care, as no disease-modifying therapy is established
Consider dietary methionine restriction to lower the hypermethioninaemia and abnormal transmethylation metabolites
Prevent and treat hypoglycaemia by maintaining glucose supply, using diazoxide where hyperinsulinism is demonstrated
Control seizures with anticonvulsants and manage the encephalopathy supportively
Monitor and support hepatic function and correct coagulopathy
Assess for cardiac involvement and provide developmental therapy and physiotherapy for hypotonia and delay
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive disorder
